disease_info: Acute Stress Disorder (ASD) is characterized by the development of anxiety, dissociative, and other stress-related symptoms within three days to one month following exposure to a traumatic event involving actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violation. Core clinical features include intrusive recollections, avoidance, negative mood, dissociation, and marked arousal, with associated functional impairment. Symptoms must arise shortly after the trauma and resolve within a month; persistence beyond this period suggests possible progression to Posttraumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD). ASD is distinguished from normative stress reactions by its severity, breadth of symptoms, and degree of interference with daily functioning, and from PTSD primarily by its shorter duration and greater emphasis on dissociative phenomena.

narrative.personality: A pragmatic, data-driven operations veteran with a competitive streak, Evan balances analytical problem-solving with outdoorsy hobbies and a relaxed tolerance for minor disorganization.
narrative.stressor: Evan was overseeing a late-night changeover at one of the manufacturing plants he manages when a malfunctioning conveyor caused a serious accident, pinning a long-term employee’s leg and nearly pulling another worker into the machinery before emergency shutoffs were triggered. As the most senior person on site, he coordinated the rescue efforts, stayed with the injured employee until paramedics arrived, and then spent the rest of the night dealing with police, OSHA, and company executives, replaying every decision that might have prevented the incident. In the days that followed, he was expected to lead the internal investigation and reassure staff, but he found himself increasingly on edge at the plant, second-guessing equipment safety and reacting intensely to routine noises and alarms, which began to interfere with his ability to make clear operational decisions and to sleep before early shifts. After three weeks of feeling constantly "on guard" at work and at home, to the point that his wife and colleagues noticed his jumpiness and uncharacteristic irritability and he began avoiding the plant floor altogether, he agreed to see a psychiatrist at his primary care doctor’s urging.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I feel like I can’t relax anywhere anymore—I’m constantly on edge, like something bad is about to happen.”

narrative.personality: Mary is a methodical, community-focused operations manager who thrives on structured planning, data-heavy spreadsheets, and nurturing others while sometimes over-organizing to feel in control.
narrative.stressor: On her way home from a late shift, Mary was driving through an intersection near her neighborhood when another car ran a red light at high speed and slammed into the vehicle in front of her, sending debris and glass across her lane and spinning the car onto the sidewalk where she had just been waiting at a previous light minutes earlier. She pulled over and, drawing on her natural tendency to take charge, called 911, directed bystanders, and stayed with an injured teenager in the crushed car until emergency services arrived, all the while acutely aware that she could easily have been in that position. Over the next several days, she tried to maintain her usual tightly scheduled routines at work and in her community volunteering, but found herself driving far out of her way to avoid the intersection, startling at sudden sounds in traffic, and feeling unable to fully relax even in familiar settings like her garden or church events, which began to affect her concentration and her willingness to drive to stores for her job. After about three weeks of feeling constantly tense on the road and noticing that her meticulous planning had escalated into excessive route-checking and avoidance that disrupted both work and family life, she decided to seek psychiatric help at her husband’s insistence when she started refusing to drive their children to activities.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Ever since that crash, I’m on high alert all the time, especially when I’m out driving—it feels like danger is around every corner.”

narrative.personality: Carl is a quietly disciplined, methodical retiree with a competitive chess player’s mind, a meticulous approach to woodworking, and a thoughtful curiosity about art and history.
narrative.stressor: Carl was out in his backyard workshop one afternoon, working alone on a large piece of oak, when a table saw kickback threw the board and dragged his hand dangerously close to the spinning blade, leaving a deep gash and narrowly missing several fingers. He managed to wrap his hand and drive himself to the emergency room, where staff told him that if the board had shifted a fraction of an inch more, he could have lost most of his hand; the combination of sudden blood loss, the noise of the saw, and the vivid explanations of potential damage left him shaken. In the weeks that followed, he tried to resume his orderly retirement routines—chess at the community center, tending his garden, and teaching basic woodworking—but each attempt to return to the workshop or even handle certain tools left him unsettled and unable to settle into his usual evening rest, with his nights becoming increasingly disrupted and leaving him tired and less engaged in his normal activities. After about three weeks of poor sleep and mounting frustration that he could no longer enjoy his woodworking or focus on reading and painting because he felt so worn down, his wife and adult daughter encouraged him to see a psychiatrist to understand why this one incident was still affecting him so strongly.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Since that accident with the saw, my sleep has been completely off—I just can’t seem to get a full, restful night anymore.”
